title: The Logic of Peter of Spain

summaries.example: Imagine the word “puppy.” By itself, it can bring the idea of a puppy to mind. In “A puppy is sleeping,” the sentence helps us know which puppies the word points to. Peter’s theory asks how words can keep a general meaning but point to different things in different sentences.
summaries.summary: Peter of Spain was the name attached to a very successful medieval book about logic. The book was called the Tractatus and later became known as the Summulae logicales. It taught students how to understand words, sentences, categories, arguments, and mistakes in reasoning. It also explained how words such as “every,” “only,” “if,” “not,” and “necessarily” affect what a sentence says. A second work, the Syncategoreumata, studied words that do not have their full effect by themselves but work together with other words. The author’s exact identity is still uncertain. Some people once thought he was Pope John XXI, while other traditions connect him with members of the Dominican order or other Peters of Spain. Researchers have ruled out some proposed identities, but they have not settled the question. The logical works probably came from southern France or northern Spain and may have been written sometime from the 1220s to the 1250s. Peter’s ideas are important because they show medieval thinkers carefully studying how language, meaning, truth, and reasoning fit together.
key_ideas: Peter of Spain wrote a famous medieval textbook called the Tractatus, or Tracts, about logic.
Scholars are still unsure exactly which Peter of Spain wrote the book.
The Tractatus explains sentences, categories, arguments, fallacies, and the ways words work in context.
Peter also wrote about special words such as “not,” “if,” “only,” “every,” and “necessarily.”
His work was copied and printed many times and used in European schools for centuries.
summaries.why_it_matters: Peter’s books show that people long ago asked questions we still ask today: What does a word mean? How does a sentence become true or false? How can a small word like “if” or “not” change an argument? Learning about his work also teaches us that historians sometimes have to investigate uncertain evidence before deciding who wrote an important book.

important_terms.definition: The study of how reasoning works and how sentences can support conclusions.
The idea that a word can stand for something in a particular sentence or situation.
A word’s general meaning, learned through the way people use it.
A word that needs other words to help give it a full role in a sentence, such as “if,” “not,” or “only.”

questions_to_think_about: Can one word have a general meaning but point to different things in different sentences?
Why might a word like “not” change the meaning of a whole sentence?
Why is it useful to study old books about reasoning?

summaries.example: Consider the pair “A person is an animal” and “A person will be an animal.” Peter distinguishes a term’s significatio—its general, conventional meaning—from its suppositio, what it stands for in a particular context. Tense can alter that contextual range. His analysis therefore treats meaning as more than a dictionary definition: logical evaluation depends on how a term functions within a proposition.
summaries.summary: The SEP entry examines the logic attributed to Peter of Spain, especially the Tractatus and the Syncategoreumata. The Tractatus combines material inherited from the older Aristotelian-Boethian logical tradition with the medieval study of the properties of terms. It discusses propositions, predicables, categories, syllogisms, argumentation, fallacies, relatives, and the theories of supposition, ampliation, restriction, and distribution. Supposition concerns what a term stands for in use, while signification concerns the word’s conventional content. Peter’s classifications show how tense, quantifiers, and other linguistic features affect reference. The Syncategoreumata belongs to a genre devoted to syncategorematic expressions: words that do not contribute their full logical function in isolation. Peter analyzes “is,” “not,” “only,” “except,” “if,” “begins,” “ceases,” modal expressions, connectives, and related terms. His treatment of composition and negation connects sentence structure with states of affairs, while his treatment of necessity grounds modal truth in necessary features of things or relations. He also holds that the conditional “if” expresses a form of causality and distinguishes different kinds of impossibility. Interpreters describe his outlook as moderately realistic, though the entry also notes an intensional emphasis on linguistic content. His theory contains tensions between universal natures and individual referents, especially in natural and simple supposition. Finally, the author’s identity remains unsettled: the attribution to Pope John XXI is not secure, and several Dominican and other candidates have been proposed or rejected. key_ideas: The Tractatus has an older logical part, drawing on Aristotelian and Boethian materials, and a later medieval part centered on properties of terms.
Its theory of supposition distinguishes a word’s general signification from what it stands for in a given context.
The Syncategoreumata studies the logical work of words such as negation, conditionals, exclusives, quantifiers, and modal terms.
Peter analyzes “is” through composition and treats negation as removing an affirmed composition rather than simply naming a different object.
His account links logical necessity and conditional consequence with states of affairs in reality, a tendency that differs from some other medieval approaches.
The entry emphasizes both the historical success of Peter’s works and unresolved questions about their author, dating, and attribution.
summaries.why_it_matters: Peter’s logic is a major example of medieval work on semantics: the study of how language carries meaning and reference. It shows that questions about context, quantifiers, modality, negation, and valid inference were developed in detailed ways before modern logic. The entry also illustrates why intellectual history requires caution. A text can be influential even when its author, date, and relationship to other attributed works remain uncertain.

important_terms.definition: A medieval theory about how a term stands for things when used in a proposition; its range can change with context.
The conventional representation or general content associated with a word.
The contextual capacity of a term to stand for particular things, including possible differences caused by tense or other expressions.
A use in which a common term stands for a universal nature rather than for particular individuals.
A word whose logical contribution depends on combination with other words, including “not,” “if,” “only,” and “necessarily.”
An enlargement of a term’s range of reference, for example when a modal expression allows reference beyond presently existing individuals.
A form of reasoning in which premises are used to support a conclusion; Peter discusses syllogism, induction, enthymeme, and example.
A view that explains linguistic expressions partly through their relation to reality outside the mind; the entry also describes Peter’s semantics as intensionalist in its attention to content.

questions_to_think_about: Should a word’s meaning be separated from what it refers to in a particular sentence?
Does “necessarily” expand the range of a term to past and future individuals, or does it require that such individuals presently exist?
What is the difference between denying a state of affairs and denying the affirmation that presents it?
Can an impossible premise support every conclusion, or only some conclusions?
How might Peter’s approach differ from a theory that treats logical terms as referring mainly to mental concepts?

summaries.example: Suppose a student says, “Every dragon is sleeping.” The word “every” seems to talk about all dragons, even if there are no real dragons. Medieval logicians asked what such a sentence commits us to. Peter of Spain’s discussion of distribution examines how universal words spread a term across the things it may stand for, and even considers the special puzzle of the phoenix, a creature traditionally described as unique.
summaries.summary: Peter of Spain is best known for the Tractatus, a medieval textbook that was taught and circulated widely in European universities for centuries. Its exact author is difficult to identify. Older accounts linked him with Pope John XXI, while other proposals connected him with Spanish or Portuguese scholars and with members of the Dominican order. Current research has removed some candidates but has not solved the puzzle. The Tractatus may have been written between the 1220s and 1250s, probably within a continental tradition associated with southern France or northern Spain. The book begins with familiar parts of older logic: nouns, verbs, propositions, categories, predicables, syllogisms, and kinds of argument. It then turns to the properties of terms. Peter distinguishes signification, a word’s general conventional meaning, from supposition, what the word stands for in a particular use. He describes several types of supposition, including uses for universal natures, for individuals, and for individuals selected or spread by expressions such as “a” and “every.” He also studies ampliation, restriction, appellation, distribution, relatives, and fallacies. The Syncategoreumata develops a related project. It examines words whose contribution depends on their connection with other terms, including “not,” “if,” “only,” “except,” “begins,” “ceases,” and “necessarily.” Peter connects these expressions with composition, negation, consequence, time, motion, and modal truth. key_ideas: The Tractatus became one of the most widely used medieval logic textbooks, surviving in many manuscripts and printed editions.
The author’s identity is disputed; the entry does not treat the identification with Pope John XXI as established.
Peter’s textbook moves from basic logical ideas to the properties of terms, including how words refer in different contexts.
His second logical work studies words that gain their full logical role only when combined with other words.
Peter’s account is connected with earlier grammar and logic, especially traditions associated with Aristotle, Boethius, Priscian, and Donatus.
His theories sometimes move between talking about universal kinds and talking about individual objects, creating interpretive problems.
summaries.why_it_matters: Peter’s work matters because it gives us a detailed picture of how medieval thinkers analyzed language and reasoning. Many of his problems still appear in discussions of reference, conditionals, negation, quantifiers, and necessity. His history also teaches an important research lesson: influence and authorship are separate questions, and strong evidence for one does not automatically settle the other.

important_terms.definition: A system for checking whether reasoning from statements to a conclusion works correctly.
The way a term stands for things when it is used in a particular sentence.
The general meaning a word has because people have assigned and use it in a certain way.
A word such as “not,” “if,” “only,” or “every,” whose logical role depends on other words in a sentence.
A sentence or argument designed to expose a difficult case or possible mistake in reasoning.
A form of reasoning in which a general claim and another claim are used to reach a conclusion.
The study of how words refer, vary in meaning by context, and affect truth and inference.

questions_to_think_about: If a sentence says “Every phoenix exists,” how should we understand “every” when only one phoenix is imagined?
Is a word’s meaning the same as what it refers to in a particular sentence?
Why might medieval logicians study ordinary words such as “if,” “only,” and “not”?
What can we learn from a book when we are not certain who wrote it?
Should logical necessity depend on language, on reality, or on both?
